metadata.file_name: Using machine learning to identify important predictors of school science literacy achievement  evidence from the United States.pdf
metadata.title: Using machine learning to identify important predictors of school science literacy achievement: evidence from the United States

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 data for the United States and constructs a school-level analytic dataset by aggregating student- and teacher-reported questionnaire variables to the school mean (students and teachers nested within schools; no multilevel modeling was used). The manuscript reports deleting missing values and retaining 238 schools, but it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the MARS estimation. Because the analysis is performed with the R caret package and a MARS model, the paper does not document any complex-survey weighting strategy (e.g., use of W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT or BRR/jackknife). As a result, the weighting approach for producing population-representative estimates is unclear, and the reported predictive performance should be interpreted as conditional on the analytic sample and preprocessing described.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 for the United States, focusing on science literacy as the assessment domain (science was the focus of the 2015 cycle). The analytic unit was the school: student- and teacher-reported questionnaire variables were aggregated to the school level by averaging across students/teachers within each school. The authors deleted missing values in the original dataset and retained the final sample of 238 schools (no outliers were found). The outcome was not discretized; the model used the continuous school science literacy outcome.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science literacy (United States; school-level aggregation)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MARS (multivariate adaptive regression spline) — RMSE: 0.63; GCV: 0.33; GRSq: 0.72; optimal model retained 16 terms with no interaction effects (main effects only).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science literacy the study leveraged Science self-efficacy, Achievement motivation, Enjoyment of science, Instrumental motivation, and Teacher feedback (among other retained predictors) to predict school science literacy achievement, finding that self-efficacy was the most powerful predictor with a sharp threshold increase once school-level self-efficacy exceeded about 1.4 SD. This indicates that school improvement priorities should focus on raising students’ collective science self-efficacy (and related motivational dispositions), while also recognizing that some instructional/practice variables show negative associations concentrated in specific regions rather than uniformly harmful effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2015 science literacy data for the United States and constructed a school-level dataset by aggregating student- and teacher-reported questionnaire variables to the school mean (238 schools after deleting missing values). The authors applied a multivariate adaptive regression spline (MARS) model with grid search over hyperparameters and 10-fold cross-validation, selecting a main-effects-only model with 16 retained terms. Predictive performance was RMSE = 0.63, GCV = 0.33, and generalized R² (GRSq) = 0.72, with 10 relatively important predictors accounting for 72% of the variance. The strongest predictor was students’ science self-efficacy, showing a steep increase beyond roughly 1.4 SD, while several teacher/student practice variables had negative associations concentrated at moderate-to-high levels. Limitations include the lack of reported complex-survey weighting/replicate design handling and the fact that predictive importance and hinge-function patterns are not causal evidence about which school actions would improve achievement.
